I’ve seen some comments about how the Cybercab can only support DC charging, which is only partially correct. The vehicle still charges via AC when wirelessly charging.

Another misconception continues to propagate that wireless charging for EVs is pointless or not viable.

That is patently false. Wireless charging already achieved speeds close to those of the Wall Charger many years ago, and Tesla’s acquisition of Wiferion was solely to acquire its technology and engineering team to advance its capabilities further.

With the same NEMA 14-50 outlet that powers the Wall Charger, you can expect 8-10kW and a fully charged Cybercab (0 -> 100%) in six hours, or 10 -> 80% (optimal battery) in four hours or less.

When Cybercab is eventually sold to customers, you can expect zero barriers to ownership: wireless charging at home and NACS fast charging when out and about.
